women.label: Women’s history
women.date_label: Nineteenth-century and interwar work; renewed expansion from the 1960s
women.description: Studies women as historical actors and examines work, family, politics, and structures of power. Earlier scholarship, activism, teaching, and documentary collecting precede the field’s expansion alongside later feminist movements. Recovery, institutional growth, rediscovery, and methodological disagreement overlap; this is not a field created from nothing in the 1960s or one account of a shared female experience.
women.representative_figures_and_works: Lucy Maynard Salmon, Domestic Service (1897); Alice Clark (1919); Ivy Pinchbeck (1930); Julia Cherry Spruill (1938); Mary Ritter Beard (1946); Eleanor Flexner (1959); Eileen Power; Dorothy Thompson; later work by Gerda Lerner and Sheila Rowbotham. Individual entries distinguish contributions and approaches. Leonore Davidoff and Catherine Hall: Family Fortunes (1987); Elizabeth Fox-Genovese: Within the Plantation Household (1988).

archival_turn.label: The archive as object
archival_turn.date_label: Le goût de l'archive 1989 · Archive Fever 1994/1996 · Silencing the Past 1995 · Dust 2001 · Archival Science 2 'archives, records, and power' 2002 · Archive Stories 2005 · 'Venus in Two Acts' 2008 · Along the Archival Grain 2009 · Dispossessed Lives 2016 · Trouillot Remixed 2021
archival_turn.description: This editorial grouping brings together distinct inquiries into archives as institutions, practices, sources and objects of interpretation. Trouillot's Silencing the Past (1995) located the silences of history in 'the making of sources', 'the making of archives', 'the making of narratives' and 'the making of history in the final instance' (as quoted by Davidson, 2020), and made the Haitian Revolution the case of an event 'unthinkable' as it happened. Stoler asked colonial historians to move 'from archive-as-source to archive-as-subject' (2002) and to read 'along the archival grain' before reading against it, finding in Dutch colonial records a 'repository of good taste and bad faith' (2009, as quoted by Gouda). Farge's Le goût de l'archive (1989), Derrida's Archive Fever (1994) and Steedman's Dust (2001) wrote the archive's allure, fever and dust; Schwartz and Cook, from the archival profession, called archives 'active sites where social power is negotiated' (2002); Burton's Archive Stories (2005) collected historians' encounters with their sources; Hartman's 'critical fabulation' (2008) and Fuentes (2016) confronted the violence of slavery's archive.
archival_turn.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier works: Arlette Farge, Le goût de l'archive (1989; The Allure of the Archives, 2013, foreword Natalie Zemon Davis); Thomas Richards, The Imperial Archive (1993); Jacques Derrida, Mal d'archive / Archive Fever (lecture 1994; Diacritics 1995; Chicago 1996); Michel-Rolph Trouillot, Silencing the Past (1995; 20th-anniversary edition with Hazel V. Carby's foreword, 2015); Saidiya Hartman, Scenes of Subjection (1997). Selected interventions: the History of the Human Sciences issue 'The Archive' (1999); Terry Cook, 'Fashionable Nonsense or Professional Rebirth' (Archivaria 51, 2001); Carolyn Steedman, Dust and 'Something She Called a Fever' (2001); Archival Science 2:1–2, 'archives, records, and power' (2002: Joan M. Schwartz and Terry Cook; Ann Laura Stoler, 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance'); Refiguring the Archive (2002: Achille Mbembe, 'The Power of the Archive and its Limits'; Stoler); From the Margins (2002: Nicholas B. Dirks, 'Annals of the Archive'); Diana Taylor, The Archive and the Repertoire (2003); Ann Cvetkovich, An Archive of Feelings (2003); Marlene Manoff, 'Theories of the Archive from Across the Disciplines' (2004); Antoinette Burton, ed., Archive Stories (2005: Durba Ghosh, Tony Ballantyne, Adele Perry, Ann Curthoys). Later contributions: Stoler, Along the Archival Grain (2009) and the Bijdragen debate (Gouda, Raben, Schulte Nordholt, 2009); Anjali Arondekar, For the Record (2009); Hartman, 'Venus in Two Acts' (Small Axe 26, 2008); Francis X. Blouin and William G. Rosenberg, Processing the Past (2011); David Zeitlyn, 'Anthropology in and of the Archives' (2012); Marisa J. Fuentes, Dispossessed Lives (2016); Trouillot Remixed (2021). Readers: Frances Gouda, Remco Raben, Henk Schulte Nordholt (2009); Alyssa Goldstein Sepinwall (2013); Marlene L. Daut (2021); Bastien Craipain (2024).
archival_turn.scope_note: A Research-field entry gathering a readership rather than a school: in the History PhD citation graph (release 2026-10-23) the share of Canada + US theses citing two or more of Stoler, Trouillot, Farge, Derrida, Hartman, Steedman, Burton, Fuentes, Blouin and Rosenberg rose from 0 (1990s) to 3.3% (2000–09), 7.1%, 7.6% and 10.4% (2020–25; US 11.8%, Canada 9.0%; Europe 2.1%), with Stoler cited by 10.7% of theses in 2020–25 across 11 of 18 fields and Trouillot by 5.9%; no opposing side is co-cited (cohorts README §5), and Along the Archival Grain entered the global/transnational neighbourhood of PhDs in 2020–25. Six strands: the archive as a site of power (Trouillot, Mbembe, Schwartz and Cook); reading along the grain (Stoler); allure, fever and dust (Farge, Derrida, Steedman); absence, violence and critical fabulation (Hartman, Fuentes); archive stories and the ethnography of archives (Burton, Dirks, Zeitlyn); the archivists' turn in Canada and South Africa (Cook, Schwartz, Harris, Brothman). Research of 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-archive.md): read in full — Gouda (2009), Schulte Nordholt (2009), Ottevaere (2004), Schultz (2015), Craipain (2024), the Chicago obituary and the finding aid for Trouillot; in part — Cook (2001), the Bulamah–Goyatá–Pereira introduction (2020), Davidson (2020); abstracts and contents only — Stoler 2002, Schwartz and Cook 2002, Mbembe 2002, Manoff 2004, Trouillot 2003, Along the Archival Grain, Archive Stories, From the Margins, Haunted by Empire, Duress, For the Record, The Archive and the Repertoire. Unread: the bodies of Silencing the Past (the four-moments passage is given as later writers list it and as Davidson quotes it, unpaginated; wording awaits re-verification on a library copy of ch. 1), Along the Archival Grain, Carnal Knowledge, Archive Fever, Dust and the AHR essay, Le goût de l'archive, 'Venus in Two Acts', Dispossessed Lives, The Imperial Archive, Processing the Past, Zeitlyn 2012, the HHS 1999 issue, Sepinwall 2013, Daut 2021, Carby's foreword. Richards (1993), Blouin and Rosenberg (2011) and the HHS issue are named in the works list but not dated as events (no page reached). Indigenous data sovereignty and the digital archive are out of scope (see web_history for the 2024 uptake of Stoler's phrase).

strands.title: The archive as a site of power: Trouillot, Mbembe, Schwartz and Cook
strands.focus: Trouillot's Silencing the Past (1995) holds that silences enter historical production at four moments — 'fact creation (the making of sources)', 'fact assembly (the making of archives)', 'fact retrieval (the making of narratives)' and 'retrospective significance (the making of history in the final instance)' (as quoted by Davidson, 2020) — and that 'in history, power begins at the source' and 'archives are the institutions that organise facts and sources' (as quoted by Davidson, 2020, unpaginated; wording awaits re-verification on a library copy of ch. 1). Craipain (2024) reads the book as a 'critical indictment of Western historiography' whose 'historical guild' relegated 'racism, slavery and colonialism' to 'an historical backburner' (Trouillot, p. 98, as quoted by Craipain). From the archival profession, Schwartz and Cook opened Archival Science's 'archives, records, and power' issues (2002) with the claim that archives 'are not passive storehouses of old stuff, but active sites where social power is negotiated' (abstract); Mbembe's 'The Power of the Archive and its Limits' (2002) begins from the archive as 'a building, a symbol of a public institution' (abstract).
strands.works: Silencing the Past (1995); 'The Power of the Archive and its Limits' (2002); 'Archives, Records, and Power' (2002)

strands.title: Reading along the grain: Stoler's ethnography of the colonial archive
strands.focus: Stoler's 2002 essay asked anthropologists in colonial studies, whose 'archival activity tends to remain more an extractive than an ethnographic one', to move 'from archive-as-source to archive-as-subject' (abstract). Along the Archival Grain (2009) treated Dutch colonial records 'not just as repositories of state power, but as unquiet movements in a field of force' (pp. 32–33, as quoted by Schulte Nordholt), looked 'for the pulse of the archive in the quiescence and quickened pace of its own production' (p. 35) and aimed 'to set a new standard for an ethnography of the archives' (p. 45) rather than an ethnography in them. Gouda: she 'underscores the necessity to read along the grain before trying to read against it, as many postcolonial scholars in recent years have advocated' (2009, p. 552). The reviewers' doubts are part of the record: Schulte Nordholt was 'not quite sure how to identify these "pulses"' and found 'an unexpected colonial flavour' in a book that ignored archives in Indonesia and Indonesian scholars (pp. 560, 562); Gouda found 'so little engagement with the work of contemporary Dutch historians' (p. 555).
strands.works: 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance' (2002); Along the Archival Grain (2009); the Bijdragen debate (2009)

strands.title: Allure, fever and dust: Farge, Derrida, Steedman
strands.focus: Three texts made the historian's experience of the archive their subject. Farge's Le goût de l'archive (1989; English 2013, with Natalie Zemon Davis's foreword) is, in Yale's words, a reflection on the sensory and emotional experience of archival work in the judicial records of eighteenth-century Paris; Arnold Hunt called it 'an eloquent testimony to the materiality of the archive and its power to astonish and delight'. Derrida's Archive Fever (lecture 1994; Diacritics 1995; Chicago 1996), already on the derrida, memory and freud entries, is 'an extended meditation on remembrance, religion, time, and technology' that starts from archiving (publisher). Steedman's Dust (2001) and 'Something She Called a Fever: Michelet, Derrida, and Dust' (AHR 106:4, 2001) answered Derrida with the archive as the repository of 'that which will not go away' and named 'archivization' as the practice of attending to it (publisher description). Terry Cook dated the 'Derrida aftershock', in which historians and others were 'subjecting the archival world to a detailed critique such as it has never before experienced', from inside the profession (2001, p. 21). All three bodies unread.
strands.works: Le goût de l'archive (1989); Archive Fever (1994/1996); Dust (2001); 'Something She Called a Fever' (2001)

strands.title: Absence, violence and critical fabulation: Hartman, Fuentes
strands.focus: Hartman's 'Venus in Two Acts' (Small Axe 26, June 2008) examines a girl's presence and silence in the archive of Atlantic slavery; the MacArthur Foundation describes her 'speculative method she terms "critical fabulation," which questions historical archives as the sole source of credible information about the past' (2019). Scenes of Subjection (1997) 'traces continuities between pre- and post-emancipation eras' (MacArthur). Fuentes's Dispossessed Lives (2016), on enslaved and free women in eighteenth-century Bridgetown, 'interrogates the archive and its historical production to expose the ongoing effects' of slavery's violence, 'combining fragmentary sources with interdisciplinary methodologies that include black feminist theory' (publisher). Both are unread here; the strand records their place in the readership (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23: Hartman 4.3% of Canada + US theses in 2020–25, from 0 in 2000–09; Fuentes a 2020–25 entrant to the US capitalism and Indigenous networks).
strands.works: Scenes of Subjection (1997); 'Venus in Two Acts' (2008); Dispossessed Lives (2016)

strands.title: Archive stories and the ethnography of archives: Burton, Dirks, Zeitlyn
strands.focus: Burton's Archive Stories (Duke, 2005) collected, in the press's words, ethnographies of the archival world by historians that challenge 'the claims to objectivity associated with the traditional archive'; its introduction is titled 'Archive Fever, Archive Stories', and its contributors include Durba Ghosh on miscegenation in Britain and India, Tony Ballantyne on 'Mr. Peal's Archive', Jennifer Milligan on 'What Is an Archive?' in modern France, Adele Perry on 'The Colonial Archive on Trial' in Delgamuukw v. British Columbia, and Ann Curthoys. Dirks's 'Annals of the Archive: Ethnographic Notes on the Sources of History' opened Part 1, 'Ethnography and the Archive', of From the Margins (2002), the volume that also printed Stoler and Trouillot. Zeitlyn's 'Anthropology in and of the Archives' (Annual Review of Anthropology 41, 2012) and Manoff's survey of 'theories of the archive from across the disciplines' (2004), which found 'a confluence of interests among scholars, archivists, and librarians', mark the turn's consolidation. All bodies unread; the strand rests on contents and abstracts.
strands.works: From the Margins (2002); The Archive and the Repertoire (2003); 'Theories of the Archive from Across the Disciplines' (2004); Archive Stories (2005); 'Anthropology in and of the Archives' (2012)

strands.title: The archivists' turn: Canada and South Africa
strands.focus: The profession's own turn ran beside and partly before the historians'. Cook names 'the pioneering postmodern archivists before Cook' as 'also Canadian, Brien Brothman and Richard Brown' (2001, n. 13). His plenary to the Association of Canadian Archivists (Winnipeg, 8 June 2001), printed as 'Fashionable Nonsense or Professional Rebirth', argued that appraisal should let archives 'acquire in its holdings multiple voices, and not by default only the voices of the powerful', while, 'as Verne Harris notes', not romanticising the marginalised (pp. 31–32), and that 'the Canadian parallel way of archival remembering through macro-appraisal may speak strongly to archivists in this new century' (p. 32). Schwartz (National Archives of Canada / Queen's) and Cook (Manitoba) then edited the 'archives, records, and power' issues of Archival Science (2002), citing Derrida and Harris, not Foucault or Stoler (reference list). Harris's South African work and Refiguring the Archive (2002) are the other pole. Perry's chapter on the colonial archive before the courts in Delgamuukw (2005) is the Canadian historians' link, unread.
strands.works: 'What Is Past Is Prologue' (1997); 'Fashionable Nonsense or Professional Rebirth' (2001); 'Archives, Records, and Power' (2002); Refiguring the Archive (2002)
